title: Rules Expression Evaluator
followUps: What is the time and space complexity of your evaluator, and where does the space go for deeply nested parentheses?
Analysts evaluate the same rule millions of times with different inputs. How would you avoid re-parsing it each time? Describe the representation you'd compile it to.
How would you add comparison operators, `and`/`or`, and a ternary `cond ? a : b` without rewriting everything? Where do they go in the precedence levels?
Rules are written by non-engineers. How would you report a syntax error or an unknown variable with a useful message and position?
Rules can be changed by analysts at any time and affect real prices. How would you version, test, and roll out rule changes safely?

interviewer.approach: Two standard approaches. (1) Recursive descent with one function per precedence level: expr := term (('+'|'-') term)*, term := unary (('*'|'/') unary)*, unary := '-' unary | primary, primary := number | identifier | '(' expr ')'. Tokenize first (numbers, identifiers, single-character operators) or scan on the fly. (2) Shunting-yard / two stacks (values and operators), treating unary minus as a separate high-precedence right-associative operator, detected when '-' appears at the start, after another operator, or after '('. Both are O(n) time and O(n) space (recursion depth or stack size bounded by nesting). Truncating division needs care in Python (int(a / b) has float issues for large values; use abs and sign, or math.trunc on exact integers) and is native in Java, C, C++, Go, Rust and JS with Math.trunc. Strong candidates design the grammar before coding and test unary minus, associativity, and variable names that share prefixes.
hints: Before coding, write down the precedence levels from lowest to highest. How might each level be its own small function?
Split the work: first turn the string into tokens (numbers, names, operators, parentheses), then evaluate the tokens.
How do you tell a unary minus from a binary one? Look at the token before it.
For left associativity, loop at each level instead of recursing on the right-hand side: 10 - 4 - 3 must be (10 - 4) - 3.
pitfalls: Right-associative evaluation (recursing on the right operand), so 10 - 4 - 3 gives 9 and 100 / 10 / 5 gives 50.
Floor division instead of truncation: Python's // and >> give -4 for -7 / 2.
Treating every '-' as binary, which fails on '-3', '2 * -x' and '--5'.
Reading variable names one character at a time, or substituting values with string replace so 'lim' corrupts 'limit'.
Single-stack evaluators that apply operators in the wrong order once precedence and parentheses mix.
Calling eval or a library, which the prompt rules out.

dimensions.name: Checking the AI's grammar and arithmetic semantics
dimensions.signals: Confirmed the AI's parser is left-associative, handles unary minus in every position (start, after an operator, after '(' and repeated), tokenizes whole identifiers, and truncates division toward zero in the chosen language. Rejected AI answers that use eval or string substitution. Could explain each precedence level of the code they submitted.

levels.1: Submitted AI code that uses eval, floor division, or right-associative parsing without noticing.
levels.2: Fixed semantic bugs only after failing tests; couldn't explain the grammar.
levels.3: Tested associativity, unary minus and negative division explicitly before trusting the AI.
levels.4: Gave the AI the grammar up front, reviewed each level against it, and explained how to extend it with comparisons or compile it for reuse.

watchFor: Using eval(), Function(), or a parsing library despite the prompt.
Python // or Math.floor for division, giving floor instead of truncation for negative results.
Recursive descent that recurses on the right operand, making - and / right-associative.
Replacing variable names in the string with their values, which breaks when one name is a prefix of another or a value is negative.
Unary minus handled only at the start of the expression.
